fusion_mis: The major aspects of fusion energy that are most commonly misunderstood by non-experts include both the benefits and drawbacks of fusion. I think among fusion proponents, there is a tendency to sell fusion has having no safety concerns, no waste issues, and no non-proliferation concerns that can provide unlimited, low cost clean energy. While I believe that fusion energy can provide reliable clean energy, I think that it will come at a relatively high cost (but still valuable and possibly competitive as  and will need to address real (but manageable) safety, waste, and non-proliferation considerations that will take engineering and policy work to address. On fusion skeptics, I think the aspects that are most commonly misunderstood are the timelines for fusion energy (often thinking fusion energy is farther off than 2035-2040) and the differences between fission and fusion (lots of conflation on safety, risk, and waste).
fusion_change_dis: I think it would want to try to have a more rational conversation around costs, benefits, and risks that help set realistic expectations for fusion energy. I worry that marketing claims made by some fusion experts will create expectations that, while they support private investment initially, may not support the substantial government policy and support necessary for commercialization and initial deployment. It the public loses trust in cost, performance, deployment timeline, or safety/waste/siting, I worry that it will be difficult to rebuilt the support for subsequent projects. Could companies saying "power on the grid in 2028 and it'll be cheaper than natural gas" could be a "too cheap to meter" for fusion energy.

fusion_mis: Many of the most mature D-T fusion concepts require substantial tritium inventories to startup and begin producing their own fuel. The global tritium resources available to supply these tritium inventories can only support a few large-scale pilot/demo plants. If these few technologies fail or are delayed before they begin breeding their own tritium for fuel, then it will require several years for the world to produce sufficient tritium to try again.
fusion_change_dis: If we continue cynically accepting that fusion is 30 years away, when it finally becomes a viable commercial source of energy, we may be socially, politically, and technologically unprepared to incorporate it into our energy mix. We should entertain the possibility of a fusion future not because it is inevitable but because if we don't, we may not be prepared to optimize its benefits.
